en: 7. Anusaya Yamaka 7.2 Mahāvāra 7.2.4.
Pariññāvāra (The Chapter on Full Understanding)
7.2.4.1. Positive Person (Anulomapuggala) He who fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust also fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion? Yes.
Or, he who fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion also fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust? Yes.
He who fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust also fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit?
He fully understands that which is associated with it.
Or, he who fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit also fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust? No.
He who fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust also fully understands the underlying tendency to views … pe … the underlying tendency to doubt? No.
Or else, he who fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt also fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust?
He fully understands that which is associated with it.
Does one who fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust also fully understand the underlying tendency to existence … pe … the underlying tendency to ignorance?
One fully understands that which is associated with it.
Or else, does one who fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance also fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust? No.
He who fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) also fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya)?
He fully understands that which is associated with it.
Or, he who fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit also fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion? No.
Does one who fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion also fully understand the underlying tendency to views ... pe ... the underlying tendency to doubt?
No. Or rather, does one who fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt also fully understand the underlying tendency to aversion?
One fully understands that which is associated with it.

He who fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) also fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya)... [and so on] ...the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya)?
He fully understands that which is associated with it (tadekaṭṭha).
Or, he who fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance also fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion? No.

He who fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya) also fully understands the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya)… [and so on] …the underlying tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya)?
No. Or again, he who fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt also fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit?
He fully understands that which is associated with it (tadekaṭṭha).
He who fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit also fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for existence ... pe ... the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.
Or rather, he who fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance also fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit? Yes.
He who fully understands the underlying tendency to views also fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes.
Or again, does he who fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt also fully understand the underlying tendency to views? Yes. ... [as before] ...
Does he who fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt also fully understand the underlying tendency to lust for existence ... pe ... the underlying tendency to ignorance?
He fully understands that which is associated with it.
Or, he who fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance also fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt? No.
He who fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for existence also fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.
Or, he who fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance also fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for existence? Yes. (Based on a single root.)
Does one who fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion also fully understand the underlying tendency to conceit?
One fully understands it as being associated with them.
Or else, does one who fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit also fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion? No.

Does one who fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion also fully understand the underlying tendency to views … pe … the underlying tendency to doubt?
No. Or, does one who fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt also fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion?
One fully understands that which is associated with it.

He who fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion, does he also fully understand the underlying tendency to existence … [and so on] … the underlying tendency to ignorance?
He fully understands that which is associated with them.

Or, he who fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance, does he also fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion? No. (The Section Based on Pairs.)

Is one who fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit, also one who fully understands the underlying tendency to views ... pe ... the underlying tendency to doubt?

No. Or conversely, is one who fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt also one who fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit?
One fully understands those [tendencies] that are associated with it.

Is one who fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit, also one who fully understands the underlying tendency to existence …pe… the underlying tendency to ignorance? No.

Or else, is one who fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance also one who fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit?
One fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit. (End of the Section Based on the Triad.)

He who fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views—does he also fully understand the underlying tendency to doubt? No.

Or else, he who fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt—does he also fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views?

He fully understands the underlying tendency to views; he fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit as far as they pertain thereto. … (End of the Section Based on Four.)

He who fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt—does he also fully understand the underlying tendency to existence, and so on, up to the underlying tendency to ignorance? No.

Or rather, he who fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance—does he also fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt?
He fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit. (The Section Based on the Pentad.)

Is he who fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence, also one who fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance? No.

Or else, is he who fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance also one who fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence?
He fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit and the underlying tendency to lust for existence. (End of the Sixfold Root.)

7.2.4.2. Positive Section (Anuloma-okāsa) Is it the case that wherever one fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, there one also fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion? No.
Or rather, is it the case that wherever one fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion, there one also fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust? No.
Is it the case that wherever one fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit? Yes.
Or conversely, is it the case that wherever one fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust?

In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit, but one does not thereby fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust. In the sense-sphere element, with respect to two types of feeling, one both fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit and fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust.

Is it the case that when one fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*), one then fully understands the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) ... pe ... the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*)? Yes.
Or conversely, when one fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt, does one then fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust?

In the case of painful feeling, and in the fine-material element (*rūpadhātu*) and immaterial element (*arūpadhātu*), one fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt, but not [the underlying tendency to sensual lust].

And from that [state], one fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*). In two of the feelings within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), one fully understands both the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to sensual lust.
Is it the case that whenever one fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*)? No.
Is it the case that whenever one fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for existence, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for sensual pleasure? No.
Is it the case that whenever one fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for sensual pleasure, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.
Is it the case that whenever one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for sensual pleasure?
In regard to painful feeling, the fine-material element, and the immaterial element, one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance,

but does not fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust. In regard to the two types of feeling within the sense-sphere element, one both fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance and fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust.
Is it the case that when one fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit? No.
Or conversely, is it the case that when one fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion? No.
Is it the case that when one fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to views ... pe ... the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes.
Or again, is it the case that when one fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion?

In the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), and in the form-sphere and formless-sphere realms, one fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt there, but one does not fully understand the underlying tendency to aversion there.
In the feeling of pain (dukkhā vedanā), one [fully understands] both the underlying tendency to doubt and...
One fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion;

and one fully understands the underlying tendency to existence. Is it the case that whenever one fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to existence?
No. Or conversely, is it the case that whenever one fully understands the underlying tendency to existence, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion? No.
Is it the case that whenever one fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.
Or conversely, is it the case that whenever one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion?

In the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), and in the form-sphere and formless-sphere realms, one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance, but not the underlying tendency to aversion.

And yet, one does not fully understand the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) therein. Regarding painful feeling (*dukkhā vedanā*), one both fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) therein and fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion therein.

Is it the case that wherever one fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*), one there also fully understands the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) …pe… and the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*)? Yes, it is.
Is it the case that when one fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit?
In the case of painful feeling, one fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt there, but one does not fully understand the underlying tendency to conceit there.

In the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), and in the form-sphere realm (rūpadhātu) and formless-sphere realm (arūpadhātu), one fully understands both the underlying tendency to doubt and [the underlying tendency to conceit] there.

One fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*). Is it the case that because one fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit, one therefore fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*)?

In two types of feeling within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), one fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit from that [feeling], but one does not [fully understand] the underlying tendency to lust for existence from that [feeling].

He fully understands. From the fine-material element and the immaterial element, he fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit and he fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for existence.
Is it the case that wherever one fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for existence, there one fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit? Yes.
Is it the case that wherever one fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit, there one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.
Is it the case that when one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*), one then fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*)?
In the case of painful feeling (*dukkhā vedanā*), one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance there, but one does not fully understand the underlying tendency to conceit there.

In the two types of feeling within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), and in the form-sphere realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless-sphere realm (*arūpadhātu*), one fully understands both the underlying tendency to ignorance and [the underlying tendency to conceit].
One fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit.
Is it the case that whenever one fully understands the underlying tendency to views, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes.
Or conversely, is it the case that whenever one fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to views? Yes ... [and so on].
Is it the case that because one fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for existence?

In the three feelings of the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), one fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt, but one does not thereby fully understand the underlying tendency to lust for existence.

In the fine-material realm (rūpadhātu) and the immaterial realm (arūpadhātu), one both fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt and fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for existence.
Is it the case that whenever one fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for existence, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes.
Is it the case that whenever one fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.
And is it the case that whenever one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes.
Is it the case that when one fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for existence, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.
Or rather, when one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance, does one thereby fully understand the underlying tendency to lust for existence?
In the three feelings of the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance there, but not the underlying tendency to lust for existence.

He fully understands. From the fine-material element and the immaterial element, he fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance and he fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for existence.

(Based on a single root. Is it the case that wherever one fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion, there one also fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit? No.
Or, when one fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit, does one then also fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion?

In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit there, but one does not fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion there.
In the sense-sphere element, in two types of feeling, one [fully understands] both the underlying tendency to conceit and the underlying tendency to sensual lust.
One fully understands [the latent tendency of ignorance], yet one does not fully understand the latent tendency of aversion from that same perspective.

Is it the case that wherever one fully understands both the latent tendency of sensual desire and the latent tendency of aversion, one also fully understands the latent tendency of views … pe … the latent tendency of doubt? No.

Or conversely, is it the case that wherever one fully understands the latent tendency of doubt, one also fully understands both the latent tendency of sensual desire and the latent tendency of aversion?

In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt therefrom, but one does not fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion therefrom.

In the two feelings of the sense-sphere element, one fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to sensual lust therefrom, but one does not fully understand the underlying tendency to aversion therefrom. In the feeling of pain...

From that [plane], one fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*), but one does not fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*).

Is it the case that wherever one fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion, one also fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*)? There is none.

Or, conversely, is it the case that wherever one fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for existence, one also fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion? No.
Is it the case that when one fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion, one then fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance?
No. Or rather, when one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance, does one then fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion?

In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance there, but one does not [fully understand] the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion.

And one fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion. In two types of feeling within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance and the underlying tendency to sensual lust, but one does not fully understand the underlying tendency to aversion there.

In painful feeling, one fully understands both the underlying tendency to ignorance and the underlying tendency to aversion, but one does not fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust there. (The section based on pairs.)

Is it the case that when one fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit, one then fully understands the underlying tendency to views ... pe ... the underlying tendency to doubt?

No. Or conversely, when one fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt, does one then fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit?
In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to conceit, but not [the others].
Then one fully understands both the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion.

In two types of feeling within the sense-sphere realm, one then fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to sensual lust, and the underlying tendency to conceit, but one does not fully understand the underlying tendency to aversion.
In painful feeling, one then fully understands both the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to aversion.
And yet, one does not fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to conceit from that [state].

Is it the case that wherever one fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to existence? No.

Or conversely, is it the case that wherever one fully understands the underlying tendency to existence, one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit?

In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for existence and the underlying tendency to conceit, but one does not fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion.

Is it the case that wherever one fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit, one there also fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance? No.

Or conversely, is it the case that wherever one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance, one there also fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit?
In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance and the underlying tendency to conceit,

but one does not fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion therein. In the two feelings of the sense-sphere element, one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance,
the underlying tendency to sensual lust, and the underlying tendency to conceit, but one does not fully understand the underlying tendency to aversion therein.

From that [plane], one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) regarding painful feeling, but one does not fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*).
(End of the section based on the triad.

Is it the case that from whatever [plane] one fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*), one thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*)? No.

Or again, when one fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt, does one then fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views?

In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views, but one does not fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion. In the sense-sphere element, in two of the [three] feelings...

Then, one fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views; yet one does not, from that [state], fully understand the underlying tendency to aversion. Regarding painful feeling, one fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to views;
yet one does not, from that [state], fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to conceit.
He fully understands … [as above] … (Based on the fourfold root.

When one fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt, does one then fully understand the underlying tendency to existence? No.

Or, when one fully understands the underlying tendency to existence, does one then fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt?

In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for existence, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to wrong view, and the underlying tendency to doubt; yet one does not, from that [plane], fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion.

Is it the case that wherever one fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to wrong view, and the underlying tendency to doubt, one there also fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance? No.

Or, when one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*), does one then also fully understand the underlying tendencies to sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), resentment (*paṭigha*), conceit (*māna*), views (*diṭṭhi*), and doubt (*vicikicchā*)?

In the fine-material sphere (*rūpadhātu*) and the immaterial sphere (*arūpadhātu*), one fully understands the underlying tendencies to ignorance, conceit, views, and doubt, but one does not fully understand the underlying tendencies to sensual lust and resentment. In the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), however...

In two types of feeling, one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance, the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt; yet one does not, from that [state], fully understand the underlying tendency to aversion.
In painful feeling, one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt.
And yet, one does not fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to conceit therein. (The section based on five.

Is it the case that wherever one fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence, there one also fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance? No.

Or conversely, is it the case that wherever one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance, there one also fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence?

In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence; yet one does not fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion therein.

In the two feelings of the sense-sphere element, one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance, the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views therein.
One fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt, but one does not thereby fully understand the underlying tendency to aversion and the underlying tendency to lust for existence.

In regard to painful feeling, one fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt, but one does not thereby fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence. (The Section Based on Six.)

7.2.4.3. Positive Person-Space (Anulomapuggalokāsa) Is it the case that whoever fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) with respect to a certain [object] also fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) with respect to that same [object]? No.

Or rather, is it the case that whoever fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion with respect to a certain [object] also fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust with respect to that same [object]? No.
Is one who fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust with respect to a certain [object] also thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit?
One fully understands that which is associated with it (*tadekaṭṭha*).
Or again, is one who fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit with respect to a certain [object] also thereby fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust? No.

Is it the case that whoever fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) with respect to a certain [object] also fully understands the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) ... pe ... and the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) with respect to that same [object]?

No. Or conversely, is it the case that whoever fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt with respect to a certain [object] also fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust with respect to that same [object]?

The person at the eighth stage (*aṭṭhamaka*)—with respect to painful feeling, the form element (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless element (*arūpadhātu*)—fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt with respect to those, but not the underlying tendency to sensual lust.

And yet, he does not fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) therein. That same person, in two types of feeling within the sense-sphere (*kāmadhātu*), fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) therein, and fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust that is associated with it.
Is it the case that whoever fully understands the underlying tendency to sensual lust therein also fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*) therein? No.

Or rather: he who thoroughly understands the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*) from a certain [plane] also thoroughly understands the underlying tendency to lust for sensual pleasure (*kāmarāgānusaya*) from that same plane?

No. He who thoroughly understands the underlying tendency to lust for sensual pleasure from a certain [plane] also thoroughly understands the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) from that same plane?
He thoroughly understands it as being associated with that [tendency].

Or again, does one who fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya) from a particular plane also fully understand the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) from that same plane? No.

Does one who fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) from a particular plane also fully understand the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya) from that same plane? No.
Or again, does one who fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit from a particular plane also fully understand the underlying tendency to aversion from that same plane? No.

Is it the case that whoever fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) with respect to a certain [object] also fully understands the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) ... pe ... and the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) with respect to that same [object]?

No. Or rather, is it the case that whoever fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt with respect to a certain [object] also fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion with respect to that same [object]?

The person on the eighth path (*aṭṭhamaka*)—in the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), and in the form-sphere and formless-sphere realms—fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt with respect to those [objects].

He fully understands it, yet he does not fully understand the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) therein. That same person, in regard to painful feeling, fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya) therein, and fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion that is associated with it.
Is one who fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion therein also fully understanding the underlying tendency to lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya) therein? No.

Or again, is he who fully understands the underlying tendency to lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya) in a particular state also fully understanding the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) in that same state? No.
Is he who fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion in a particular state also fully understanding the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya) in that same state?
He fully understands it to the extent that it is applicable.

Or again, is it the case that whoever fully understands the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) in a particular [plane] also fully understands the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) there? No.

Is it the case that whoever fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) in a particular [plane] also fully understands the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) … pe … the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) there? No.
Or again, is it the case that whoever fully understands the underlying tendency to doubt in a particular [plane] also fully understands the underlying tendency to conceit there? No.
